# RoboPuppy – project reference

Starting point for each Claude conversation. Updated at the end of every session.

## Goal
A Labrador-sized robotic dog built from 3D-printed and laser-cut parts. The robot is designed around its actuators. It must be able to trot dynamically.

**CAD tool: SolidCraft.** The model is generated by Node scripts (see Tooling).

## Requirements (from the owner)
- Torso about 60 cm long; everything else scaled to an average dog of that size.
- Legs: 3 axes each (hip abduction, hip pitch, knee).
- Head: 2 axes. Tilt is at the base of the neck (the whole neck nods); pan is at the top of the neck. Neck is short (about 92 mm).
- Tail: 2 axes (wag and lift), both at the tail root.
- Empty bay in the middle of the torso for battery and electronics (contents decided later).
- Exposed mechanical look for now; no cosmetic body shell.
- Fabrication available: FDM printer with 300 mm+ bed, laser cutter (wood/acrylic), and metal/carbon sheet through an external service.

## Decisions so far
- **Leg actuators:** 12× RobStride 02, classic CAN version (owner's decision, 2026-11-21; replaces the RobStride 01). 17 N·m peak, 6 N·m rated, about 405 g, Ø78.5 × 45.5 mm, 48 V rated, 24–60 V range, 410 rpm no-load at 48 V. It has the same front face and output flange as the RS01, but a bigger, longer rear cover and a different rear screw-head layout. Its speed advantage over the RS01 comes only from the higher voltage. It costs about the same as the RS01 from the sellers found. Accepted budget is roughly EUR 1,600–1,900 for all actuators. The CAD uses the RS02 (`robstride02.sc`, checked against the official STEP file). Its power connector is two XT30(2+2) sockets in the rear-cover rim, pointing outward on opposite sides; the model carries an estimated keep-out for each mated plug. Comparison of all RobStride models, prices and the CAN vs CAN FD reasoning: `docs/robstride_comparison.md`.
- **Head and tail actuators:** four Feetech STS-family serial bus servos (STS3215 class for head pan and both tail axes, a stronger one of the same size for neck tilt). Modelled as 45 × 24.7 × 35 mm bodies from memory of the datasheet; dimensions not yet verified. They need about 12 V, so a step-down converter from the battery, rated for 60 V or higher input.
- **Neck:** tilt servo lies on top of the deck at the front (ahead of the hip carriers' sweep); a printed neck (yoke, 45 mm tube at 45°, cradle) carries the pan servo.
- **Head:** hollow printed shell (skull 110 × 100 × 85, muzzle 95 × 56 × 48, 2.5 mm walls) on the pan servo horn. One camera behind each eye, 64 mm apart; keep-out sized for a Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 (assumption until the computer is chosen). The rest of the head is left empty for future additions.
- **Tail:** wag servo hangs under the rear tip of the deck spine with its shaft up through the deck; it carries the lift servo; the tail is a flexible 300 mm TPU rod on a yoke.
- **Leg architecture:** abduction actuator fixed to the torso; hip-pitch actuator held in a printed carrier; knee actuator on the thigh, coaxial with the hip pitch, driving the knee through a 1.5:1 belt (HTD 5M, 15 mm wide, 635 mm long, 24:36 teeth) between two thigh plates. The shank blade swings beside the belt, not in its plane.
- **Thigh plates:** 3 mm aluminium, laser-cut (owner's choice for now; carbon would save about 0.55 kg in total).
- **Hip spacer:** a printed horseshoe (RP-108, 35 mm thick, the full gap between the plates) ties the two thigh plates together around the hip, where one plate is on the hip-pitch actuator and the other on the knee actuator. Seven of the nine knee-actuator front screws pass through both plates and the spacer; the two lowest hold only the outer plate (shared 9-hole pattern). Two through-bolts at its leg ends replace the two upper standoffs. The bore (Ø56) and the open bottom clear the belt and the hip pulley.
- **Two knee drive variants:** the linkage knee in the style of Unitree (`leg_linkage.sc`, `robot_linkage.sc`) is now the main design, carrying the new leg below. The belt knee (`leg.sc`, `robot.sc`, above) is frozen as a reference at its old 242 mm links (owner's decision, 2026-11-22): it still builds, but gets no new work. The owner has not formally dropped it.
- **Linkage leg (the main design; first shaped in the motion rig, carried into the part files on 2026-11-22):** the Unitree Go2 is the reference.
  - **Lengths:** thigh and shank 200/200 mm (`lt`, `ls`; the Go2 is 213/213), standing in the Go2's pose (hip 45.8°, knee −85.9°). The robot is about 370 mm tall, with the feet about 320 mm below the hip axes, roughly 15 mm behind them.
  - **Four-bar:** the knee actuator turns a 22 mm crank (RP-114, 5 mm aluminium). A pushrod (RP-115) with an M5 rod end at each end runs down the rear of the thigh to the lever pin at the top of the shank, 28 mm from the knee at −12° from the shank axis. Rod 203 mm (lt + 3). Knee fold 60–159°. Ratio 1.38 standing, 1.27–1.38 over the trotting folds (86–105°), at least 1.25, about 3.0 at 60° and 2.1 at 159°; transmission angles at least 18°. The crank can only sweep about 144°, so the ratio is set mainly by the fold range. Rod length sets the knee zero; there is no tensioner.
  - **Pushrod and rod ends (owner's decision, 2026-11-22):** the pushrod is an 8 × 4 mm 6061 tube (T6 expected; listings often just say "6061"). The 4 mm bore is opened to the 4.2 mm tap drill at each end and tapped M5 directly, so no end plugs are needed. It takes male SA5 T/K rod ends, not female rod ends on a thinner steel rod. At 203 mm it buckles at about 3.1 kN, against about 1 kN worst-case rod force (3.3 kN for solid Ø8), and weighs about 21 g. A thin stainless rod is heavier for the same buckling strength, an M5 threaded rod would buckle near peak torque, and female rod-end bodies would eat the clearance to the knee tube and between the shank plates. Use 8–10 mm thread engagement, jam nuts and threadlocker. Planned: one left-hand rod end so the rod works as a turnbuckle.
  - **Thigh (reshaped 2026-11-22 from the owner's sketch):** two 3 mm aluminium plates (RP-111 inner, RP-112 outer), 20 mm apart, shaped like a hook that bends near the knee. Hip round R42 and knee round R20, joined by four tangent arcs. The rear edge is two convex arcs: R1200 (nearly straight) from the hip, then R230 into the knee from 0.4·lt below the hip. The front edge is two concave arcs: R210 from the hip round, then R40 into the knee from 0.75·lt. The folded shank nests in front of the bend. The owner's sketch had the front edge about 15 mm behind the hip–knee line. It was limited so the plate always covers the rod, with at least 1.5 mm in front of it at every fold; the front edge reaches about 7 mm behind the line. Narrowest about 34 mm, just above the knee. Five M3 × 20 standoffs (four behind the rod, one in front near the hip), each at least 6.9 mm inside the edges. The printed hip spacer (RP-113) is the front of the hip disc, trimmed to the upper front arc, with a bore round the crank hub; four knee-actuator screws clamp it (each at least 2.8 mm from its edges). Knee axle (owner's decision, 2026-11-23): a hardened sleeve 5 × 8 × 20 (bearing steel quenched to 58–62 HRC, outside ground 8 0/−0.01; sold as a wear sleeve), clamped between the thigh plates' inner faces by a Chicago screw M4 × 25 (Ø5 barrel, grip 25–27 mm, stainless 18-8, heads about Ø10 × 3, estimated) through both plates. The needle bearing runs straight on the sleeve. The owner wanted the axle bolted at both ends, so plates that bend or spread with use cannot leave it unsupported at one end; the clamp also ties the two thigh plates together at the knee. Earlier options were ruled out: tapped hardened shafts (tapping anneals the ends, per Misumi), a plain shaft held by printed keepers (not bolted), an INA IR 5 × 8 × 16 inner ring (needs spacers), and shoulder screws (class 12.9 is only about 40 HRC and f9, too soft and loose for the needles, and still needs the sleeve). The barrel only takes shear (about 64 MPa worst case); the sleeve carries the bending (about 150 MPa worst case, hardened steel). The knee holes are cut at Ø4.8 and reamed to 5 H7, as at the lever pin (so the barrel overlaps each plate by the 0.1 mm ream allowance in clash checks, intended); plate bearing stress on the barrel about 37 MPa at the trotting peak, 83 MPa worst case.
  - **Shank:** two identical 3 mm aluminium plates (RP-118, 26 wide), 9 mm apart and 2.5 mm inside the thigh plates. Each follows a gentle S-shaped centreline (reshaped 2026-11-22 from the owner's sketch): a 15 mm line from the knee leaning 4° to the rear, an R150 arc turning toward the front, then an R175 arc turning back to the foot under the knee. It is about 1 mm behind the knee line near the knee and about 15 mm in front of it at mid-length. The plate top is a round (R16) about the axle joined to a boss (R11) round the lever pin. Between the plates: the printed knee hub (RP-122, see Knee pivot) and two M3 × 9 standoffs on the centreline, 55 and 125 mm along it from the knee.
  - **Lever pin (owner's decision, 2026-11-22):** a Chicago screw (sex bolt) M4 × 15 with low heads (barrel Ø5 × 15; barrel head Ø8.5 × 1.8, screw head Ø8.3 × 1.7) through both shank plates and the rod-end ball (double shear), with a DIN 988 5 × 10 × 0.5 shim each side of the ball. From about 60° to 105° of knee fold (standing and trotting included) the pin passes under the thigh plates, so only low heads fit. That is why the shank plates went from 10 to 9 mm apart: the heads now clear the thigh plates by 0.7 and 0.8 mm. The barrel length must equal the stack (2 × 3 + 9 = 15 mm); the build checks this. The pin hole is modelled at its cut size, Ø4.8 (`cs_d - ream_stock`), and reamed to 5 H7 after cutting, so the pin does not hammer the hole as the rod load reverses. Holes finished by reaming are always modelled at the cut size (cad-modelling skill, §3), so the cut file needs no extra instruction. The pin therefore overlaps each shank plate by 4.6 mm³ in clash checks (intended).
  - **Shank plate material and strength (owner's decision, 2026-11-22):** 5754-H22 or better (the owner's laser-cutting service uses 5754 by default; H111 also works, with less margin). Rod force at the actuator's 17 N·m peak is 0.78–1.0 kN over 70–140° of fold, rising to 2.3–2.5 kN at the fold ends; each plate takes half. With the R11 boss and the reamed Ø5 hole, the hand estimates per plate are: worst case about 25 MPa net, 60 MPa peak at the hole edge and 83 MPa bearing; fast trot (reversing) about 25 MPa peak at the hole edge. That gives a fatigue margin of about 2 (allowing half for fretting). In H111 the worst-case margin is about 1.3. 5754 is softer than 6061-T6, so the hole wears faster against the steel barrel: grease it and check for play. A worn hole can be reamed to 6 mm and sleeved.
  - **Knee pivot (owner's decision, 2026-11-22; bushings replaced by a needle bearing the same day):** one drawn-cup needle bearing, INA/SKF HK0812-2RS (8 × 12 × 12, sealed both ends; distributors list C about 2.7 kN, C0 about 2.6 kN), pressed into a printed PETG knee hub (RP-122) and running straight on the hardened knee sleeve. Ball bearings were ruled out: the pushrod passes 10.4 mm from the knee axis at full fold (159°), between the shank plates, and the ball bearings that fit (MR128, MR148) have static ratings of only 0.28–0.39 kN, against an axle load of about 1.1 kN at the trotting peak and 2.5 kN at the fold ends at peak torque. The needle bearing has a static margin of about 2.4 at the trotting peak and about 1 at the worst case, almost no friction (the bushings would have cost about 0.6–1 N·m at the knee) and a few hundredths of radial play. The owner chose a printed hub to avoid lathe parts. The hub's body (Ø26, 9 mm, between the shank plates) is cut back to R9.3 between −35° and 73° in the shank plate frame (0° forward, 90° up), where the rod passes at deep folds (1 mm clearance at 159°); elsewhere the wall round the bearing is about 7 mm, 3.3 mm at the relief. A D-shaped spigot (Ø18, flat 7.5 mm behind the axis) at each end sits in the matching laser-cut hole in each shank plate, which keys the hub so the relief stays toward the rod; the plates clamp the body through the shank standoffs. Spigot bearing stress on the PETG: about 2 MPa standing, 11 MPa at the trotting peak, 26 MPa worst case. Bearing makers want drawn cups in metal housings; in PETG the press fit may relax, and the remedy is a new print. Sideways: needle bearings take no axial load, so each side has a DIN 125-A M8 washer (16 × 1.6) against the hub end and DIN 988 8 × 14 shims (0.5 + 0.2) against the thigh plate, leaving 0.2 mm play each side (the build checks that the lever pin heads keep at least 0.3 mm); adjust the shims at assembly.
  - **Foot (owner's decision, 2026-11-22):** a printed core (RP-120, Ø44 × 24) inside a printed TPU ring (RP-121, Ø56). Both have two slots that take the plate ends. The slots follow the plates' last arc (R175), with 0.2 mm clearance, and end in a round about the foot centre. An M4 bolt through the core and both plates holds it. RP-106 (the belt leg's pad) could not be shared, because the plates pass through the ring.
  - **Knee:** at 159.8° the foot pad meets the thigh's hip end, so the lying-down pose has the feet against the hips. The fold starts at 60° rather than 50° to raise the knee ratio.
  - **Knee torque (hand estimate, 12.5 kg):** RS02 actuator about 2.8 N·m standing, 10–11 N·m peak in a slow trot, 12–14 brisk, 14–16 fast, and about 5.3 N·m RMS in a slow trot (rated 6). The knee can deliver about 22–23.5 N·m (1.8 N·m per kg; the Go2 has about 3.0). Leg reach is about 346 mm fully extended, against 293 mm standing. With the old linkage leg (242 mm links, 45–140°) the RMS was above the rating and brisk trots hit the 17 N·m peak.
  - **Left and right:** the S-shaped shank is not symmetric front to back, so the right-hand lower leg is the mirror module of the left (same part files in mirrored positions). Every leg part passes the mirror-symmetry check.
  - **Results:** width over the knee actuators 303 mm (belt: 333). The hip carrier, actuators, torso, neck, head and tail are shared with the belt variant.
- **Link lengths:** linkage (main design) 200/200 mm; belt variant 242.2/242 mm (`lt_belt`, `ls_belt`; the thigh is set by its 635 mm belt). Back height about 370 mm standing (belt robot about 470 mm).
- **Hip layout:** the thigh plane is 42 mm outboard of the abduction axis so it clears the abduction actuator and the torso. Abduction axes are 42 mm either side of the centreline. Hip pitch axes are 420 mm apart front to rear.
- **Width:** 333 mm over the knee actuators with the belt; 303 mm with the linkage (each 10 mm more than with the RS01, from the longer rear cover).
- **Torso:** each pair of abduction actuators is clamped between a bulkhead and a mid frame (3 mm aluminium). A printed belly pan spans between the mid frames; a 2 mm aluminium deck closes the top and extends as a spine to the neck and tail. Each spine end is stiffened by a bent 3 mm aluminium angle rib (front RP-205, 174 mm; rear RP-206, 125 mm, stopping 1 mm short of the tail wag servo), screwed to the deck along the centreline. The rib root passes through a slot in the bulkhead up to the mid frame. Lower corners are rounded about the abduction axes and the top is only 120 mm wide, so the thighs can swing past. The abduction actuators' plugs point straight up and down: they pass through a slot in the deck and a notch in the belly pan, and the mid frame has a notch and a tab under each actuator.
- **Knee direction:** all four knees bend backward.
- **Battery:** 13S2P Li-ion (owner's decision, 2026-11-21; replaces the 10S plan), using 26 high-drain 21700 cells (5 Ah, 25 A or more continuous). 46.8 V nominal, 54.6 V full, 39 V empty. 468 Wh nominal, about 375 Wh usable, about 2.1 kg (+1.3 kg over the old 10S1P plan). Estimated 1.7–2.8 h trotting. Estimated draw at 11 kg is 40–60 W standing, 120–200 W trotting and 0.5–1 kW peaks, scaled up with mass. The model still has the old 200 × 110 × 72 battery keep-out; resizing it is next (HANDOFF.md). Regen with a full pack can exceed the RS02's 60 V limit (braking resistor, or charge to 4.1 V per cell). Details and the 3P/4P comparison: `docs/battery.md`.
- **Shared parts across sides:** the assembly is mirrored left to right, but every fabricated part must be the same on both sides (owner's rule). Parts are symmetric or work turned over. The hip carrier has the actuator hole pattern every 60°, a plug slot top and bottom, and rear holes and head pockets for both hands, so one carrier fits all four hips.
- **Joint directions:** hip pitch and knee turn about +Y on every leg; positive abduction is outward on both sides. Actuator convention (true for the RS02): a dowel pin and a front M3 hole in line with the plug, M4 holes 30° off.
- **Mass:** target about 11 kg; current estimate 10.8–11.5 kg (the hip spacers and spine ribs added about 300 g; the head shell is about 230 g and the tail 137 g if solid; all of these should be lightened). Not yet redone for the RS02, the 13S2P pack or the new linkage leg (the knee torque estimate assumes 12.5 kg).
- **Joint limits found so far (all four legs driven together):** abduction outward about 17° for now, because the hip-pitch actuator's top plug swings into the deck spine from about 18° (the owner left the fix for later; the carrier itself meets the deck at about 32°); inward, the front and rear legs on the same side collide at 36°. Knee fold 145° with the belt (from the old model); 60–159° with the linkage leg (full robot and rig). Abduction and hip pitch are still ±45° and ±120° placeholders on the linkage leg.

## Tooling
- **Modelling rules** are in the `cad-modelling` skill (`.claude/skills/cad-modelling/SKILL.md`; the owner plans to move it to the personal skills folder). In short: one file per part, reuse by instancing, same parts on both sides, fully constrained sketches, one sketch and one hole feature per hole group, patterns and mirrors for repeats.
- **Models are generated, not hand-edited.** Node scripts in `cad/scripts/` write command scripts to `cad/*/build/` (git-ignored) and run them in SolidCraft. Run from the repo root:
  - `node cad/scripts/build.js all --app` builds every part, then all four assemblies and the motion rig. `parts <key>` builds one part; `leg`, `robot`, `leg_linkage`, `robot_linkage` or `rig` one assembly. A dims.js key ending in `_ang` becomes an angle parameter (degrees); every other key a length.
  - `node cad/scripts/build.js symmetry [keys] --app` checks that every part used on both sides equals its own mirror image.
  - `node cad/scripts/build.js check robot` (or any assembly key) runs a clash check on the saved assembly; with `--app` it also writes renders to its `build/` folder.
  - `node cad/scripts/build.js pose [assembly] HipAbduction -45 45` drives that joint on all four legs to each angle and clash-checks that robot there (default `robot`). Without `--app` it runs one CLI script on the saved file and does not save it back.
  - `node cad/scripts/build.js ping [words] --app` tests the connection and lists app commands matching the words.
  - A part build fails if any sketch is not fully constrained.
- **How Claude reaches SolidCraft:** the CLI (`C:\Program Files\SolidCraft\solidcraft-cli.exe`) and the `solidcraft` MCP connector (a headless session; it can only open files inside the repo) both run now; Windows Smart App Control blocked them in earlier sessions because SolidCraft's Windows builds are unsigned (their issue #8317). Builds without `--app` use the CLI. `--app` instead sends the command scripts to the open desktop app over its local control channel (`cad/scripts/lib/control.js`; TCP port in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SolidCraft\control\current.port`, with a token file next to it), which needs Preferences > Assistant > "Let AI agents connect" on. Each `--app` build runs in a new tab, saves, and closes that tab; the owner's tabs are left alone. Renders need the app or the MCP (`screenshot`).
- `.claude/settings.local.json` exempts `node cad/scripts/build.js *` from the Claude Code sandbox so the build can reach the app's port.
- The app re-saves every part file it rebuilds, and .sc files are binary, so a full rebuild shows every part as changed in git.
- **Generator files:** `dims.js` (every dimension, passed to the part files as named parameters), `parts.js` (one definition per part), `assemblies.js` (leg modules, both variants of the leg and robot), `rig.js` (the motion rig), `build.js` (runner), `lib/` (sketch helpers, placement maths, four-bar maths in `linkage.js`, the linkage leg's plate outlines in `legshape.js`, control-channel client).
- **`lib/legshape.js`** holds the thigh and shank plate outlines (geometry and sketch commands) for both the part files and the rig, so the two cannot drift apart. Its sketch commands go into a sketch of their own (ids start from 1). The thigh outline's arc centres are found by a numeric scan; the shank centreline by Newton iteration, so that the foot lands under the knee. The sketch constraints then place the geometry exactly.
- **How assemblies are structured:** SolidCraft flattens a linked assembly file (its part list and joints are lost), so only part files are linked. The leg is defined once in `assemblies.js` as three rigid modules (hip, thigh, lower leg), plus a crank module and a rod module for the linkage variant. In the robot, modules are local sub-assemblies placed twice or four times: two hip modules and two thigh modules (one per hand), and one lower leg (belt, turned half a turn for the right side) or two (linkage: the S-shaped shank is handed, so `LowerLeg_L` and `LowerLeg_R`). A right-hand module places the same part files in mirrored positions; the build refuses a mirrored part.
- **Linkage loop in SolidCraft:** crank–thigh and rod–crank are revolute joints, rod–lever a ball joint, made after the knee is driven to the standing pose (where the crank and rod were placed). Driving a knee moves the crank and rod; the crank angles match the four-bar maths to 0.01°. `joint.find_limits` stalls on the linkage (the rod ends touch the crank and lever face to face), so knee checks use discrete poses.
- **SolidCraft cannot drag grouped legs with the mouse (known limitation).** A click in the view, with any selection filter, picks the part inside a sub-assembly (for example LowerLeg_L:1 → ShankPlate:1). The app then refuses the move silently ("no joint places it: it is not connected to anything grounded"), because it does not treat that part as moving with its parent's joints. Driving joints by value, and moving the sub-assembly itself (`joint.reach` on LowerLeg_L:1), both work. The same happens in the single-leg files. Only a flat layout (parts directly in the top assembly) would allow mouse dragging in SolidCraft; the owner rejected that for the real assemblies, so the motion rig below is a separate study model for dragging.
- **Motion rig (`cad/robot/motion_rig.sc`, built by `rig.js`):** the linkage robot made to be dragged with the mouse, for finding joint limits and trying leg changes. The torso is the real parts, linked into one grounded component. Each leg is five top-level components built in the file from plain bodies: hip (carrier and hip-pitch actuator with plugs, one definition for all four), thigh (hook-shaped plates, spacer, standoffs, knee actuator), shank (two S-shaped plates with their tops, knee hub, spacers, foot), crank and pushrod (hollow, 8 × 4). Thigh and shank each have left and right definitions. Every size comes from `dims.js`, and the plate outlines from `lib/legshape.js`, as in the part files; the rig's bodies are envelopes (no holes, bushings or foot slots). Limits: abduction ±45°, hip pitch ±120°, knee −159 to −60°. The crank and rod follow the knee through the four-bar. Saved in the Go2 standing pose (hip 45.8°, knee −85.9°). Every dims.js name its sketches use is a live parameter (`lt`, `ls`, `lk_a`, `lk_b`, `lk_ang`, the thigh and shank outline radii, ...); `lk_c` is `lt + 3` there, so the knee zero follows `lt`. The legs follow a change, but joint limits are plain numbers (the app does not re-read a limit expression). A change found in the rig goes into `dims.js` to reach the part files. It is a study model: not in any BOM, and its handed links break the shared-parts rule on purpose.
  - **Live contact is too slow for it,** so the rig is saved with its "Collisions" contact set switched off. With contact on, every drag fails with "motion exceeds contact sweep intersection budget" after a freeze of several seconds, because jointed neighbours with sub-mm clearances slide past each other. Switch contact on in the app only to probe one limit. A one-off `contact.check` with the set enabled works but takes about 70 s. `build.js pose rig` switches contact off first in case it was saved on.
  - **Checking the leg:** 2D side-view checkers (not in the repo) found the linkage, the free space for standoffs and the fold limit: first one in Python (shapely), then, for the reshape, one in Node. The Node one traced the owner's sketch, fitted the arc radii and junction heights to it, and rendered SVG to PNG with headless Edge; shapely and PIL are not installed here. `node cad/scripts/build.js pose rig Knee <angles>` clash-checks the rig. Its output lists every body pair, including bodies within the same link (first occurrences carry no component tag), so filter for pairs from different links by the body-name prefix. `pose robot_linkage Knee <angles>` checks the real parts.
  - **Sketch naming for the shank plates:** `sketch.offset` of a three-curve chain (line, arc, arc) with `symmetric: true` gives `l2, a3, a4` on the + side (points p1–p4, knee to foot) and `l3, a5, a6` on the − side (p5–p8).
- **Four-bar maths (`lib/linkage.js`):** `knee(q, geometry)` and `ratio(q, geometry)` take an optional geometry (crank, lever, rod, lever angle, thigh length); without one they use the `dims.js` values (`lk_a`, `lk_b`, `lk_c`, `lk_ang`, `lt`).
- **Foot slots:** near the foot the shank plates still curve (R175), so a straight slot in the foot core and pad clashed with them by up to about 0.5 mm. The slots are now the plate's own arc band plus clearance (centre at (`sh_r2`, 0) in the foot frame), and the foot parts are turned so their +Y follows the plate's tangent at the foot.
- **Reading the owner's selection:** the control-channel method `ui.selection` returns what is selected in the open app (`selection.get` through `engine.execute` sees only the headless selection, which is empty).
- Named views (`view.apply {view: ...}`) frame the renders oddly; check the model visually in the app.
- Interference checks can run long: use `engine.batch` (one-hour timeout), not `engine.execute` (60 s).

## Repository layout
- `cad/parts/` – one design file per unique part (46 files: 29 for the belt robot, 16 for the linkage leg only, and the unused `robstride01.sc`, kept by the owner's choice), purchased parts and keep-out volumes included. The printed linkage shank (RP-116, `shank_lk.sc`) was removed when the plate shank replaced it.
- `cad/leg/` – single-leg assemblies (`leg.sc` and `leg_linkage.sc`, front-left leg on a bulkhead), render and BOMs.
- `cad/robot/` – whole-robot assemblies (`robot_linkage.sc`, the main design, and `robot.sc`, the frozen belt variant, each saved in its standing pose), the motion rig (`motion_rig.sc`), renders and BOMs (`bom_linkage.csv`, 33 items; `bom.csv`, 27 items).
- `cad/scripts/` – generators.
- `cad/actuators/` – older RobStride 01 reference model; the assemblies use `cad/parts/robstride02.sc`. `cad/actuators/build/` (git-ignored) holds local copies of the official RS01 and RS02 STEP files (licence not checked, so not committed).
- `docs/` – design notes: `robstride_comparison.md` (actuator specs, prices, purchase options, CAN vs CAN FD, RS02 fit check) and `battery.md` (13S2P pack sizing).
- **No production files in the repo** (owner's decision): DXF, 3MF and STEP exports go to `cad/*/export/`, which is git-ignored, and are only produced once the whole design is complete. The export step has not been rewritten for the new part files yet.
- Superseded, kept for now: `cad/leg/leg_module_concept.sc`, `cad/robot/robot_blockout.*`, `cad/scripts/gen_blockout.js`.

## Current state
First detailed pass, in linked part files. The whole robot is one articulated assembly (16 joints): a detailed torso, four detailed legs with real bolt patterns, and a neck, head and tail built around servo positions. The main design has the linkage knee and the new 200/200 mm leg; the belt variant is kept, frozen at 242 mm links. Every sketch is fully constrained and every part used on both sides passes the mirror-symmetry check. Nothing has been printed or cut.

Earlier sessions switched the model to the RobStride 02 and added the motion rig, where the owner redesigned the leg: 200/200 mm links in the Go2 stance, a hook-shaped thigh, a shank of two S-shaped aluminium plates, a knee folding 60–159° (feet against the hips when lying down) and a retuned four-bar (ratio about 1.3–1.4 while trotting). The pushrod became an 8 × 4 mm aluminium tube. Then the new leg went into the part files and both linkage assemblies. `lt`/`ls` became 200/200 and the belt variant got its own `lt_belt`/`ls_belt`. The thigh plates (RP-111/112), the hip spacer (RP-113) and the crank (RP-114, now 22 mm and 5 mm thick) were reshaped. New parts came in: the shank plate (RP-118), the knee spacer tube (RP-119), the foot core (RP-120), the slotted TPU foot pad (RP-121), the shank standoffs and flanged knee bushings. The printed shank RP-116 is gone. The rig takes every size from `dims.js` and its plate outlines from the same code as the part files (`lib/legshape.js`).

In the latest session the lever pin was designed and modelled: a low-head Chicago screw M4 × 15 with a shim each side of the rod-end ball (new purchased parts `chicago_screw_m4x15.sc` and `shim_5x10.sc`). For the heads to clear the thigh plates, the shank plates moved to 9 mm apart (2.5 mm inside the thigh plates), so the shank standoffs became M3 × 9 (`standoff_m3x9.sc`, replacing M3 × 10). The knee tube and the foot slots follow the new gap. The shank plate's pin boss grew from R8 to R11 and its pin hole is now cut Ø4.8 and reamed to 5 H7 (`ream_stock` in `dims.js`). The plate material is now in its description (5754-H22 or better). The rig takes the shank plate positions from `dims.js` (they were typed numbers) and has the screw heads. Checks: symmetry of every new and changed part; the linkage robot shows only the known clashes at knee folds of 60, 70, 85.9, 100, 115, 130, 145, 155 and 159° (plus, after the pin hole went to its cut size, the intended 4.6 mm³ overlap of each lever pin with each shank plate); the rig has no clashes between links at the same folds.

## Coordinate convention
X forward, Y left, Z up. Origin at the torso centre, at the height of the hip abduction axes. Leg-local frame: origin where the abduction axis meets the hip pitch axis, Y outward. Each part file has its own frame, described in a comment above the part in parts.js.
